title: Word order and focus
seoTitle: Turkish word order, focus and inversion
intro: Turkish word order is free, but not random. In a neutral sentence the verb comes last; the word right before it is the focus, the new or important part; what follows the verb is already known. Speakers move words in and out of these slots to do what English does with stress or with **it was … who**. This unit also covers topics, echo words such as *kitap mitap*, and the small words that add emphasis.

sections.title: The focus slot before the verb

blocks.text: A neutral Turkish sentence ends with its verb: subject, then time and place, then object, then verb ([A1 unit 8](gp-object-word-order)). The position right before the verb is special: it holds the **focus**, the part of the sentence that is new or contrasted, and it carries the main stress. Change what you put there, and you change the question the sentence answers.

head: Sentence
It answers
Meaning
rows: It was Ali who bought the book yesterday.
Ali bought the book at the bookshop yesterday.

blocks.text: **Questions and answers.** A question word sits in the focus slot (*Kitabı kim aldı?*), and the answer puts its new word in the same place (*Kitabı Ali aldı*). In speech you will often hear only that word: *Ali.* The particle `mI` marks the same slot in a yes-no question ([A1 unit 4](gp-question-mi)): *Kitabı Ali mi aldı?*, was it Ali who bought the book?

**The bare object goes with its verb.** An indefinite object with no case ending is glued to its verb, and the two count as one unit, so the focus slot moves one step to the left: *Dün akşam kim kitap okudu? — Ali kitap okudu.* Without a contrast, the pair itself is the news: *Ali dün akşam kitap okudu* (Ali spent last evening reading).

**Contrast and değil.** To deny one element and give another, put it in the focus slot of a negative verb, or in front of *değil*: *Kitabı Ali almadı, Ayşe aldı* (it wasn't Ali who bought the book, it was Ayşe), *Ben değil, Ayşe aldı* (not me, Ayşe bought it).

**Clefts.** For heavier emphasis, Turkish turns the rest of the sentence into a participle ([B1 unit 5](gp-headless-an)) and puts the focus in the predicate: *Kitabı alan Ali'ydi* (the one who bought the book was Ali), *Beni en çok şaşırtan, fiyatı oldu* (what surprised me most was the price), *Asıl önemli olan, türkünün yaşaması* (what really matters is that the folk song lives on).

lines.en: Your mother? And there I was thinking it was you!

lines.tr: Ben değil, annem. Ben sadece yedim.
lines.en: Not me, my mother. I just ate it.

items.tr: Kitabı dün Ali aldı.
items.seg: Kitab|ı dün Ali al|dı.
items.en: It was Ali who bought the book yesterday.

items.tr: Kitabı Ali mi aldı?
items.seg: Kitab|ı Ali mi al|dı?
items.en: Was it Ali who bought the book?

items.tr: Toplantıya ben değil, Selin gidecek.
items.seg: Toplantı|y|a ben değil, Selin gid|ecek.
items.en: It's Selin who'll go to the meeting, not me.

items.seg: Bu şehr|e ilk kez geçen yıl gel|di|m.

items.tr: Beni en çok şaşırtan, fiyatı oldu.
items.seg: Ben|i en çok şaşırt|an, fiyat|ı ol|du.

blocks.text: To find the focus of a sentence you read, look at the word just before the verb, then ask which question the sentence answers.
English moves the stress (**ALI** bought it) or uses a cleft (**it was Ali who…**), as French uses **c'est … qui**. Turkish usually just moves the word.

In speech, words often come **after** the verb: *Geldi mi Ayşe?* (has Ayşe come?), *Gördüm onu!* (I saw him!), *Çok güzeldi film* (the film was really good). Grammar books call this an inverted sentence (*devrik cümle*). It is not an error: the words after the verb are background, already known or added as an afterthought, while the verb and what comes before it carry the news.

**What can go there.** Subjects, definite objects, adverbs and whole phrases can follow the verb: *Aradın mı babanı?*, *Gidiyorum ben*, *Gelirim yarın*. What cannot: the focus, so never a question word (*Kimi gördün?*, not *Gördün kimi?*), and a bare object, which stays glued to its verb (*Kitap okudum*, not *Okudum kitap*; but *Okudum kitabı* is fine).

head: Neutral
Inverted
What the inversion does
rows: asks about the arrival; Ayşe is already the topic
puts the news first, with feeling
a reaction; everyone knows which film
the time added as an afterthought

blocks.text: **Where you meet it.** Inversion is everywhere in conversation; in songs and folk poetry, where it serves rhythm and rhyme; and in literary prose, for effect. In formal writing, such as reports, articles and letters, keep the verb at the end.

items.tr: Gördün mü yeni komşuyu?
items.seg: Gör|dü|n mü yeni komşu|y|u?
items.en: Have you seen the new neighbour?

items.tr: Bitti mi ödevin?
items.seg: Bit|ti mi ödev|in?
items.en: Is your homework finished?

items.tr: Çok yoruldum bugün.
items.seg: Çok yorul|du|m bugün.
items.en: I'm so tired today.

items.tr: Ben söylemiştim sana!
items.seg: Ben söyle|miş|ti|m sana!
items.en: I told you so!

items.tr: Nereye gidiyorsun bu saatte?
items.seg: Nere|y|e gid|iyor|sun bu saat|te?
items.en: Where are you going at this hour?
items.note: The question word stays before the verb; *bu saatte* is background.

blocks.text: Keep the verb last in formal writing, and never put a question word after the verb: *Kimi gördün?*, not *Gördün kimi?* In everyday speech a bare object stays before its verb too: *Kitap okudum*, not *Okudum kitap*.

Folk verse bends even these rules for the rhyme. In an old Istanbul mani of this unit's interlude, *Nerden içsin kuzu su*, both the subject and the bare object follow the verb; everyday Turkish would say *Kuzu nereden su içsin?*

The start of a sentence usually holds the **topic**, what the sentence is about: it is already known, and the comment follows. A definite noun at the start is usually the topic: in *Bu filmi çok sevdim*, the film is what we are talking about, and *çok sevdim* is what we say about it. Turkish also has markers for a topic, especially one that contrasts with another or opens a new subject.

head: Marker
Use
Example
rows: *Ben çay içtim, Ayşe ise kahve.* / *Ayşe'yse kahve içti.*
turning to a new topic: as for

blocks.text: **İse and -(y)sA.** You met *ise* as **whereas** in [B2 unit 3](gp-contrast-connectors). The same particle marks a contrasted topic: it comes right after the topic, before the comment. Attached as `-(y)sA` it sounds more everyday: *Ali İzmir'e gitti, ben ise Ankara'ya* or *bense Ankara'ya*. After a case ending: *Bana ise kimse sormadı* or *Banaysa kimse sormadı* (as for me, nobody asked).

**-(y)A gelince.** *Gelince* (when it comes, [B1 unit 7](gp-ince)) after a dative turns the conversation: *Bana gelince…* (as for me), *Paraya gelince, o başka bir konu* (as for the money, that's another matter). It often announces a contrast with what was just said.

**-DAn yana** frames a topic as an area: *Paradan yana sorunumuz yok, zamandan yana var* (money's not a problem for us; time is). **Topic and focus together.** A typical sentence runs from topic to focus: in *Kardeşimse dün akşam bize geldi*, *kardeşimse* is the contrasted topic and *bize*, right before the verb, the new information.

items.tr: Ben çayı şekersiz içerim, eşim ise üç şekerli.
items.seg: Ben çay|ı şeker|siz iç|er|im, eş|im ise üç şeker|li.
items.en: I take my tea without sugar, whereas my wife takes it with three.

items.tr: Herkes erken gitti; Mehmet'se sabaha kadar kaldı.
items.seg: Herkes erken git|ti; Mehmet'|se sabah|a kadar kal|dı.
items.en: Everyone left early; Mehmet, though, stayed until morning.

items.tr: Bana gelince, ben bu işe karışmam.
items.seg: Bana gel|ince, ben bu iş|e karış|ma|m.
items.en: As for me, I'm staying out of this.

items.tr: Paradan yana sorunumuz yok, zamandan yana var.
items.seg: Para|dan yana sorun|umuz yok, zaman|dan yana var.
items.en: Money's not a problem for us; time is.

items.tr: Yemeklere gelince, hepsi buz gibiydi.
items.seg: Yemek|ler|e gel|ince, hep|si buz gibi|y|di.
items.en: As for the food, all of it was stone-cold.

blocks.text: *İse* and `-(y)sA` follow the topic word; they never open the clause: *Ayşe ise kahve içti*, not *ise Ayşe kahve içti*. And don't mistake the topic `-(y)sA` for a condition: here *Mehmet'se* means **as for Mehmet**, not **if it's Mehmet**; the context decides.

sections.title: Kitap mitap, ıvır zıvır: echo words

blocks.text: Turkish loves pairs of words. One kind anyone can make: repeat a word with its first consonant replaced by *m*, or with *m* added before a first vowel, and you get **… and the like, … and all that**, often with a shrug: *kitap mitap* (books and that sort of thing), *çay may* (tea or whatever), *okul mokul* (school and all that). TDK writes the pair as two words, the second one without a meaning of its own.

**What it means.** The pair stands for the thing and everything like it, and the tone is casual, often dismissive: *Kitap mitap istemiyorum, biraz dinlenmek istiyorum* (I don't want books or anything, I want a rest). *Okul mokul derken yıl bitti* (what with school and all that, the year was over). A word that already begins with *m* can't be doubled this way; use *falan* instead ([B2 unit 9](gp-fillers)): *masa falan*, *müzik falan*.

**Fixed pairs** (*ikilemeler*). Besides the m-pairs anyone can make, Turkish has hundreds of fixed pairs: echoes whose second word means nothing on its own (*ıvır zıvır*, *eğri büğrü*, *abur cubur*), near-synonyms (*eş dost*, *konu komşu*, *çoluk çocuk*), opposites (*az çok*, *er geç*, *aşağı yukarı*) and sound words (*şırıl şırıl*, *mışıl mışıl*). TDK writes most of them as two words; a few are one (*darmadağın*, *çerçöp*, *öteberi*).

head: Pair
Meaning
Example
rows: Çantamda bir sürü ıvır zıvır var.
Bu haberi bütün konu komşu duydu.
the whole family, children and all

blocks.text: M-doubling is casual and can sound dismissive. Leave it out of formal writing, and be careful with things the listener cares about: *Düğün müğün umurumda değil* tells the bride you don't care about her wedding.
English has a few echo pairs (helter-skelter, higgledy-piggledy) and the Yiddish-flavoured **fancy-shmancy**, which works just like m-doubling.

sections.title: Ta, hem de, de mi, işte: adding emphasis

blocks.text: Speech adds weight with small words as much as with stress. You know *dA*, *hem de* and *işte* from [B2 unit 8](gp-da-particle); here they work as emphasis, with one newcomer, *ta*.

head: Word
What it stresses
Example
rows: how far, or how long ago: all the way, as far back as
*Ta İstanbul'dan geldi.* (He came all the way from Istanbul.)
*Bu, aradığım kitabın ta kendisi!* (This is the very book I was looking for!)
and what's more; and at that
*Kazandık, hem de beş sıfır!* (We won, and five-nil at that!)
surprise or reproach: too, even, again
*Bugün de mi geç kaldın?* (You're late again today?)
*İşte bu yüzden gelmedim.* (That's exactly why I didn't come.)

blocks.text: **Ta** (pronounced with a long a) stretches a distance or a time, and goes with `-DAn`, *-(y)A kadar* or *beri*: *ta Ankara'dan* (all the way from Ankara), *ta sabaha kadar* (right through till morning), *ta çocukluğumdan beri* (ever since I was a child). *Ta kendisi* is **the very one**; *ta ki* brings in a final limit, **until at last**: *Bekledi de bekledi, ta ki kapı açılana kadar* (she waited and waited, until at last the door opened). It is written apart and has nothing to do with the locative: *ta İstanbul'dan*, but *İstanbul'da*.
**Hem de** adds a stronger point after a statement: *Geldi, hem de erkenden* (she came, and early at that). On its own, *Hem de nasıl!* is **and how!**

**dA mI** asks, in surprise or reproach, whether something applies **too**, **even** or **again**: *Sen de mi?* (you too?), *Bunu da mı bilmiyorsun?* (you don't even know this?), *Bugün de mi geç kaldın?* (late again today?). The particle stands after the word it highlights, and `mI` follows *dA* in harmony with it: *da mı*, *de mi*.

**İşte** points at something as the very thing: *İşte bu!* (that's it!), *İşte o zaman anladım* (it was then that I understood). Before *bu yüzden*, *böyle* or *o zaman* it works like an English cleft.

items.tr: Ta Kars'tan düğüne geldiler.
items.seg: Ta Kars'|tan düğün|e gel|di|ler.
items.en: They came all the way from Kars for the wedding.

items.tr: Onu ta çocukluğumdan beri tanırım.
items.seg: O|n|u ta çocukluğ|um|dan beri tanı|r|ım.
items.en: I've known him since I was a small child.

items.tr: Bütün sınavları geçti, hem de hepsini yüksek notla.
items.seg: Bütün sınav|lar|ı geç|ti, hem de hep|si|n|i yüksek not|la.
items.en: She passed all her exams, and every one with high marks at that.

items.tr: Bu sene de mi tatile çıkmıyorsunuz?
items.seg: Bu sene de mi tatil|e çık|mı|yor|sunuz?
items.en: Aren't you going on holiday this year either?

items.tr: İşte o zaman her şeyi anladım.
items.seg: İşte o zaman her şey|i anla|dı|m.
items.en: It was then that I understood everything.

items.tr: Bu şarkı, çocukken dinlediğim türkünün ta kendisi.
items.seg: Bu şarkı, çocuk|ken dinle|diğ|im türkü|n|ün ta kendi|si.
items.en: This song is the very folk song I listened to as a child.

blocks.text: In writing, stress can't be seen: word order and these particles show where the weight of a sentence falls.

summary: The verb comes last; the word right before it is the focus, the new or contrasted part: *Kitabı Ali aldı* answers **who**.
Question words and the words that answer them sit in the focus slot; `mI` marks it in a yes-no question: *Kitabı Ali mi aldı?*
Words after the verb are background or afterthought: *Geldi mi Ayşe?* Never put a question word there, and keep a bare object before its verb.
Inverted sentences (*devrik cümle*) belong to speech, songs and poetry; formal writing keeps the verb last.
Topics come first; *ise*, `-(y)sA` and *-(y)A gelince* mark a contrasted or new topic: *Bana gelince…*, *Mehmet'se…*
M-doubling (*kitap mitap*) means **… and the like**, casually; fixed pairs such as *ıvır zıvır*, *eş dost* and *er geç* are learned whole.
*Ta*, *hem de*, *dA mI* and *işte* add emphasis: *ta İstanbul'dan*, *hem de nasıl*, *Sen de mi?*, *İşte bu!*
